standard.title: Wave and Particle Models
standard.description: use wave and particle models to describe energy transfer through different mediums and examine the usefulness of each model for explaining phenomena
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can explain how light travels in straight paths and describe reflection and refraction (AC9S5U03). They can explain energy transfer and transformation in electrical circuits (AC9S6U03) and classify energy as kinetic or potential (AC9S8U05). They can use particle theory to explain physical properties of substances (AC9S7U05). They have encountered both particle and wave ideas separately but have not yet applied them as competing or complementary models for explaining energy transfer, or evaluated which model is more useful for a given phenomenon.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students use wave and particle models to describe how energy is transferred through different mediums — including sound, heat and light — and examine the usefulness and limitations of each model for explaining phenomena including electromagnetic radiation.

nodes.label: The particle model of energy transfer — conduction and convection
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain conduction and convection using the particle model, describing how particle motion and collisions transfer energy through matter.
nodes.minimum_width: Students explain conduction as energy transfer through particle collisions in a solid, and convection as bulk movement of particles carrying energy in a fluid.
nodes.typical_width: Students apply the particle model to explain why metals conduct heat well (closely packed particles, efficient collision transfer) while insulators do not; explain convection currents as density-driven particle movement; connect to AC9S7U05's particle theory; describe how First Nations Australians' traditional clothing and bedding exploit or minimise conduction and convection.
wider: Investigate insulation designs from First Nations Australians' clothing and bedding across different climate regions — what particle-level mechanisms do the materials exploit?
Design a fair test comparing the insulating properties of two materials and explain the results using the particle model
nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The particle model applied to heat transfer has rich investigative width — insulation design, material comparison, traditional technologies — and the First Nations clothing/bedding elaboration is explicitly named. These are genuine contexts that extend the model without acceleration.

response_modes.reason: Students have prior particle theory (AC9S7U05) applied to physical properties but not to energy transfer. Explicitly connecting particle motion to energy transfer — collision as the mechanism, not just 'heat moves through the material' — establishes the particle model as an explanatory tool before the wave model is introduced.
Conduction and convection in varied material and cultural contexts build the model's explanatory range before it is compared with the wave model.

success_criteria: Explains conduction using particle collisions as the transfer mechanism
Explains convection using bulk particle movement driven by density differences
Applies the particle model to explain why a named material is a good conductor or insulator

nodes.label: The wave model of energy transfer — sound
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe sound as a wave and explain how sound energy is transferred through a medium using the wave model, including the relationship between wave properties and sound characteristics.
nodes.minimum_width: Students describe sound as a longitudinal wave and explain that it requires a medium, using compression and rarefaction to describe how energy is transferred.
nodes.typical_width: Students relate frequency to pitch and amplitude to loudness; model wave transfer using a slinky spring; explain why sound cannot travel through a vacuum; describe how the medium's properties affect sound transmission speed; investigate sound transmission in First Nations traditional instruments.
wider: Investigate how material selection affects sound energy transfer in a First Nations traditional instrument — explain the design choices using the wave model
Compare sound transmission speed in air, water and solids and explain the differences using particle spacing and bonding
nodes.hinge_reason: The wave model of sound is the first full application of wave properties (frequency, amplitude, wavelength, medium-dependence) as a coherent framework. Students who do not secure the wave model for sound cannot extend it to electromagnetic radiation in N4, and cannot evaluate which model is more useful for which phenomenon — the descriptor's core analytical demand.

response_modes.reason: Students have encountered sound in everyday contexts but not as a formal wave model with defined properties. Establishing wave properties (frequency, amplitude, wavelength, medium-dependence) through sound — the most concrete wave context — is the scaffold for the more abstract electromagnetic wave model in N4.

success_criteria: Describes sound as a longitudinal wave requiring a medium
Uses compression and rarefaction to explain how sound energy is transferred
Relates frequency to pitch and amplitude to loudness with examples

nodes.label: The particle model of electricity — static charge and current
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain static electricity and electrical current using the particle model of charge, and connect particle behaviour to concepts of voltage, conductors and insulators.
nodes.minimum_width: Students explain static electricity as the accumulation of charge due to electron transfer, and electrical current as the flow of electrons through a conductor.
nodes.typical_width: Students explain charging by friction, induction and contact using electron transfer; describe current as directed electron flow driven by voltage; explain conductors as materials with free electrons and insulators as materials without; connect to electrical circuit concepts from AC9S6U03; explain electrostatic discharge as rapid electron movement to neutralise charge imbalance.
wider: Investigate an electrostatics phenomenon (lightning, Van de Graaff generator) and explain it fully using the particle model of charge
Examine how semiconductor materials — with intermediate conductivity — challenge the simple conductor/insulator binary, and explore applications in electronics

response_modes.reason: Students have prior knowledge of circuits (AC9S6U03) but at the observable level — components, connections, current as a functional concept. The particle model reframes current as electron flow and extends the model to static electricity, which has no circuit equivalent. This is a model extension, not revision.

success_criteria: Explains static electricity as electron transfer between materials producing charge imbalance
Describes electrical current as directed electron flow through a conductor
Distinguishes conductors from insulators using the particle model (free vs bound electrons)

nodes.label: The wave model of light and electromagnetic radiation
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe light and electromagnetic radiation as waves and explain how the wave model accounts for phenomena including reflection, refraction and the electromagnetic spectrum.
nodes.minimum_width: Students describe light as a transverse wave and use the wave model to explain reflection and refraction.
nodes.typical_width: Students describe the electromagnetic spectrum as a family of transverse waves varying in frequency and wavelength; explain that all EM waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum; connect wave frequency to energy (radio → microwave → infrared → visible → UV → X-ray → gamma); explain how EM wave properties determine their use in communication technologies; apply the wave model to explain reflection and refraction from AC9S5U03.
wider: Investigate the forms of electromagnetic radiation used in different modern communication technologies — what wave properties make each suitable for its application?
Examine how the wave model explains UV damage to skin and X-ray imaging — what wave property is the key variable?
nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The electromagnetic spectrum connects to communication technology, medical imaging, and the wave-particle duality elaboration — all explicitly named in the elaborations. Each application context exercises the wave model in a distinct domain.

response_modes.reason: Applying the wave model across the full EM spectrum — from radio to gamma — and to real communication and medical technologies builds the model's explanatory range needed for the 'usefulness' evaluation in N5.

success_criteria: Describes light as a transverse wave and the EM spectrum as a family of waves differing in frequency and wavelength
Uses the wave model to explain reflection and refraction
Explains how wave frequency relates to energy across the electromagnetic spectrum

nodes.label: Evaluating model usefulness — wave vs particle for different phenomena
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can evaluate the usefulness of wave and particle models for explaining different energy transfer phenomena and identify where each model succeeds or fails.
nodes.minimum_width: Students identify one phenomenon better explained by the wave model and one better explained by the particle model, and explain why in each case.
nodes.typical_width: Students systematically evaluate wave and particle models against phenomena: sound (wave model — medium required, wave properties), conduction (particle model — collision mechanism), light (wave model accounts for diffraction, reflection, refraction; particle model explains photoelectric effect); introduce the concept of photons as a case where neither model alone is sufficient; explain that models are tools with domains of usefulness, not literal descriptions.
wider: Research the wave-particle duality of light — what experimental evidence supports each model, and how does the concept of photons attempt to reconcile them?
Evaluate the particle model of light (photons) for explaining the photoelectric effect and discuss what this reveals about the limits of classical models

response_modes.reason: This node is the descriptor's 'examine the usefulness of each model' demand. Students bring both models — particle (N1, N3) and wave (N2, N4) — into comparative evaluation across phenomena. The key conceptual move is recognising that models are domain-specific tools, not universal truths.

success_criteria: Evaluates the usefulness of each model for at least two distinct phenomena
Identifies at least one phenomenon where the wave model is more useful and one where the particle model is more useful
Explains that scientific models are tools with domains of usefulness rather than literal descriptions of reality
